title: Designing a social network graph

facts.text: A user searches for someone and sees the shortest path to that person; the service must be highly available.
Assumptions: traffic is uneven, some searches are more popular than others, the graph data will not fit on a single machine, and graph edges are unweighted.
The scale is 100 million users with 50 friends each on average, giving 5 billion friend relationships, and 1 billion friend searches per month, or 400 search requests per second.
The exercise avoids graph-specific solutions such as GraphQL or a graph database like Neo4j; without that constraint, a graph database or graph query language could be used.
Without millions of users (vertices) and billions of friend relationships (edges), a general breadth-first search (BFS) would solve this unweighted shortest path task.
Users cannot all fit on one machine, so they are sharded across Person Servers, which are accessed through a Lookup Service.
The client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Search API server, which forwards to the User Graph Service.

The User Graph Service asks the Lookup Service for the Person Server holding the current user, retrieves that user's friend_ids, and runs a BFS with the user as source and the friend_ids as adjacent nodes.
For each adjacent node it must again ask the Lookup Service which Person Server stores that id, a step with potential for optimization.
The public API is REST; internal communication could use remote procedure calls.

Person data can be served from a memory cache such as Redis or Memcached, which cuts response times and downstream traffic at 400 average read requests per second (higher at peak), especially for repeated searches and well-connected people.
Complete or partial BFS traversals can be stored in the memory cache to speed later lookups, or computed offline in batch and stored in a NoSQL database.
Reduce machine jumps by batching friend lookups hosted on the same Person Server, and shard Person Servers by location, since friends generally live closer to each other.
Run two BFS searches at once, one from the source and one from the destination, then merge the two paths.
Start the BFS from people with many friends, since they more likely shorten the degrees of separation to the target, and set a time or hop limit before asking the user whether to keep searching.
